description: The knowledge base for the real-time sales-call assistant. The rep types what the prospect just said; the app fuzzy/semantic-matches it against `triggers`, then surfaces `response_steps` in order. Built from the full Cole Gordon transcript corpus (134 channel videos + 19 hand-processed sources). Every response line is verbatim or near-verbatim from the source material.

universal_framework.rule: Every objection runs through the same opening before the specific rebuttal: DIFFUSE, then ISOLATE whether it is an UNCERTAINTY objection (a true objection) or a LOGISTIC (money / support / timing). Handle uncertainty FIRST, always.
universal_framework.funnel_order_note: When more than one objection fires, handle them in this order — uncertainty before any logistic. Timing is a logistic, but Cole reframes it as a priorities/certainty problem, so timing objections live in the uncertainty bucket and are handled as true objections (there is no separate timing bucket). 'process' (prospect taking control) is an app-level call-control bucket outside Cole's 3-bucket objection model — it is handled before the objection phase, not during it.
universal_framework.step_2_isolate: Just so I can stay organized on my end — when you say [their objection], are you more in a 'should I do this' place where you're not even 100% certain this is what you want, or a 'how can I do this' place where you're 100% certain and it's just a matter of logistics? (For a financial objection the isolate is value-vs-budget instead: do you not see the value, or do you want it and it's purely the money?)
universal_framework.step_3_temp_check: Money / [objection] aside — how do you feel about the process? Do you feel like this is 100% what you need to get to [their outcome], that it's 100% going to work, and that now is 100% the right time?
universal_framework.step_4_scale: What's really important to me is alignment — we're rolling up the sleeves with you, so what matters is you feel good about the process. Just to be 100% clear — on a scale of one to ten, one being 'I hate this guy, get me off the phone,' ten being 'that's exactly what I need' — where do you fall out exactly? ... What's keeping you from being a nine or a ten?
universal_framework.step_5_double_tie_down: So [objection] aside — is there anything else keeping you from being less than 100% certain that this is the right thing and now is the right time? ... So you're 100% in?
universal_framework.smoke_screen_note: 'I want to think about it' / 'it's too expensive' are usually smoke screens. The job is to turn the intangible objection into a tangible one you can actually handle. If they waffle ('I think so'), that is a NO — cut in playfully and call out the tonality. CRITICAL: a logistic (money / support / timing) handled while uncertainty is still unresolved is itself a smoke screen — if you handle a spouse before doing uncertainty first, you're handling a smoke screen.
universal_framework.concession_rule: Never give better terms (a payment plan, an extension, a deposit) for free. Trade every concession for a decision now: 'If I'm willing to do that for you, are you willing to move forward right now?' Going lower again? Also ask for a case study AND a commitment to show up and do the work. People who pay more up front get better results — they burn the boats — so pitch the full price first and use payment terms only as closing leverage.
universal_framework.loop_back_rule: After every prospect answer -- lower your tone and ask 'Hold on -- why though?' / 'Why do you feel like that?' / 'Why do you agree?' Go 5-7 LAYERS deep, not one. The first 'why' gets the rehearsed answer; the fifth 'why' gets the truth. Reps quit after 1-2 cycles; the move is to keep looping until they run out of cover and tell themselves the real answer. Different probe for mid-sentence interjection: 'Hold on -- what caused you to say that?' / 'Let me pause you for a moment.' Only interject if pain gap is built and trust is there -- otherwise = steamrolling. (Jeremy Miner / NEPQ -- the universal probe.)
universal_framework.open_vs_closed_gate: Before any direct handle (temp-check, scale, double tie-down), assess: is the mask off? Tells = emotional words, personal story, real why behind a number, conceded hidden numbers ('about a million... well, $40k last month'). If mask OFF -> direct frames work. If still ON (surface answers, scripted-sounding objections) -> soften FIRST: 'Sure, no problem. Just so I know what questions you'll have when we talk again -- what was it you were wanting to go over in your mind?' Cole: that question extracts the real objection sideways -- 'I need to see if we have the budget' -- now it's a money objection, not a think-it-over.
universal_framework.four_levels_of_persuasion: Jeremy Miner's persuasion ladder. L1 Features/Benefits (where 99% of reps live -- never wins big deals). L2 Behaviors ('what does the entrepreneur who makes $2M/yr actually DO?'). L3 Beliefs (catch the words they use -- 'at least', 'I think' -- and reframe). L4 Identity (people do who they believe they are -- Freud). Pitch from L3/L4: 'sounds like you're the type of person who never gives up -- were you born that way or did you have to learn it?' locks the new identity so they can't object without contradicting themselves.
universal_framework.permission_recover: After a sharp directness move (consequence math, identity callout, past-pain probe), pause and re-license: 'are you OK with me saying that?' Keeps the content sharp without losing them. If they interject your hard question: 'hold on -- you interjected right when I was about to give you an answer you didn't want. Why did you do that?' Names avoidance directly instead of letting them route around it.
universal_framework.operator_mindset: Cole + Jeremy's license to push: 'I'm not doing this TO them, I'm doing this FOR them — so they overcome their stories and get what they want.' Internally: 'I'm concerned about the CONSEQUENCES if they don't change' — not concerned about closing them. Reps who hold this frame come across as moral authority / fiduciary care. Reps who don't sound combative even when the words are right. Tonality leaks the frame — you can't fake it.
universal_framework.concerned_tone: Cole/Jeremy's specific tone variant (distinct from 'lower at end of question'). Same words, two tones: judgmental ('what's the version of you NOW, man?' = broy) vs concerned (softer, slower, hand-on-chest energy). PHYSICAL ANCHOR: hand on chest produces the tone — even on audio. You can't fake it from the neck up. DAILY-LIFE DRILL: use concerned tone in non-sales conversation ('how do you mean by stress?' with partner). Builds muscle so it fires automatically.
universal_framework.negative_identity_close: Jeremy Miner — AFTER the laddered why-chain ('why? ... why though? ... where do those people end up?'), close the loop with the NEGATIVE identity rejection: 'you don't sound like the type of person who [wants the bad outcome they just named].' Different from the positive identity-shift ('type of person who never gives up'). This asks them to DISOWN the failure they just described. Pair: ladder why → prospect names the failure → 'you don't sound like the type of person who [that outcome]' → 'so what do you really want?'

situations.label: Prospect went quiet / one-word answers
response_steps: Call out the silence directly, with warmth: 'Hey — you got quiet on me there. What's going through your head right now?'
Don't push the close into the silence. Re-engage first: 'Be straight with me — what's really going on? Earlier you said this is what you need. Something shifted — what is it?'
Once they name it, that's the real objection — handle it through diffuse -> isolate.
situations.do_not: Don't keep pitching into a dead line, and don't read silence as a yes. A quiet prospect is the call dying — surface what changed before you do anything else.

situations.label: Energy dropped — flat 'yeah', 'sure', 'mm-hm'
response_steps: Name the tonality playfully: 'I can hear the energy dropped a little — and that's totally fine. Let's just be honest with each other: what's really going on?'
Re-anchor to their own words: 'Earlier you told me [their goal / their pain]. Is that still true? Because right now it doesn't sound 100%.'
If they waffle, feed them the objection — it's usually nerves: 'It sounds like a bit of nerves — is it?' Then handle nerves.
situations.do_not: Don't ignore a flat 'yeah' and treat it as agreement. Flat tonality is a no — surface it now, not after the price drop.

situations.label: Hedging — 'I think so', 'probably', 'we'll see'
response_steps: Cut in playfully and call out the hedge: 'I think so? That doesn't sound 100% certain — so let's just be honest with each other, what's really going on?'
Push for the real answer: 'Do you 100% think this will work, and do you 100% want to do this? If it's not a clear yes, that's fine — but tell me what's in the way.'
A hedge is a NO until proven otherwise. Turn the intangible into a tangible objection you can handle.
situations.do_not: Don't let a hedge slide into a booked follow-up. 'I think so' is not a yes.

situations.label: Prospect is hostile / rude / 'you're just a salesperson'
response_steps: De-escalate and reset the frame: 'I hear you — and I'm genuinely not here to sell you. I'm here to see if this is a fit. If it's not, I'll tell you straight and point you in the right direction.'
Match-then-lower their energy: stay calm, lower your tone, don't get defensive. Treat it as a puzzle, not a threat.
Take responsibility if the call slipped: 'That's my bad — I think I got ahead of myself. Let's slow down. The main thing is [their problem] — talk to me about that.'
situations.do_not: Don't argue back or get defensive. A combative prospect is testing whether you'll fold or stay in the lead — stay calm and stay in the lead.

situations.label: Pause right after the price — before any named objection
response_steps: Hold the silence. After the price, do not talk first. Let them react.
If they ask 'how much was that again?' — re-anchor to the outcome, don't just repeat the number: 'The investment to take you from [current] to [outcome] is [price].'
Then ask the temp check: 'How are you feeling about it?' — and handle whatever objection surfaces.
situations.do_not: Don't fill the post-price silence with a softener, a discount, or a payment plan. The first one to talk loses leverage.

situations.label: Prospect is emotional / vulnerable / opened up
response_steps: Slow down and hold the moment — don't rush to close on top of it: 'I really appreciate you sharing that. That takes guts.'
Chase it gently: 'Tell me more about that — how's that been showing up for you?'
Tie it to the decision when the moment settles: 'That right there is exactly why this matters. So let's make sure we fix it.'
situations.do_not: Don't pounce on an emotional moment with a hard close, and don't brush past it. Sit in it, then bridge to the decision.

situations.label: Prospect joined with camera off -- get it on without being creepy
response_steps: Don't ask 'can you hear me' -- they can. Ask the confused version: 'How well can you hear me? My mic was acting up on the last call.'
Then act confused about their video: 'Is your video broken? I can't see you.' Forces them to correct the record ('no it's not broken') -- and socially they almost have to turn it on.

If they admit they always keep it off, go playful: 'Dude, what's going on, it's 12:45 over there -- you still in your pajamas? If I'd known I would have worn my underwear on here.' Playful tone -> they laugh and turn it on.
situations.do_not: Don't say 'I want to see who we're working with' -- creepy. Don't say 'is your camera off' -- accusatory, not confused. The whole move is the CONFUSED tonality.

situations.label: 'This sounds great' / 'I really want to do this' — enthusiastic tone but the BUT is loaded
response_steps: Don't celebrate — Cole: 'You know the but's coming.' Enthusiasm + no payment question = pre-objection setup.
Interject BEFORE the but lands: 'Hold on — why do you feel like you really want to do this?' Forces them to sell themselves on the program in their own words before the objection forms.
Listen to the TONE of THAT answer. Certainty ('man, I have to do this') → closer to a real yes. Soft ('well, I mean, it sounds good...') → the BUT is still coming, handle it now.

Cole tell: 'I really want to do this. Where do I pay?' = real. 'This sounds great, I really want to do this...' (trailing) = BUT incoming. Catch it BEFORE they speak the objection into existence — once spoken they have to defend it.
situations.do_not: Don't treat enthusiastic-sounding language as a buy signal — the tone tells you whether the next sentence has a BUT. Run the why-loop first.

objections.label: It's too expensive / I can't afford it / that's a lot of money
triggers: don't know if I can afford
a lot of money for this
that's just a lot for me right now
it's just a lot for me right now
almost as much as a new car
got to see if I can afford it
response_steps: No problem. Now, just to stay organized on my end — when you say you can't afford it, are you more in a 'should I do this?' kinda place where you're not even sure this is what you want to do? Or more of a 'how can I do this?' place where you're 100% certain you want to do this, it's just a matter of making it work financially? (This isolates uncertainty smoke-screen vs genuine financial logistic.)
Gotcha. So if I'm hearing you correctly — money aside, you're 100% in? (Only do the rest of this AFTER you have the double tie-down.)

Look — most of my clients do the investment up front. But for certain clients in situations where they really want to do it, it's just the money — we break it up. So given you're 100% in and it's really just about finding a way to make it work financially — are you open to exploring the option of that? (This gets permission to go into payment plans. It's why we don't offer payment plans straight away.)

[They say 'sure, what does it look like?'] Well, that depends — everything is customised based on what you need. So are you open to having an honest conversation financially and putting everything out on the table, so we can see if there's any possibility of doing this now — or at the very least we can create a game plan to work towards this in the future? (Frames the open wallet in their best interest, with permission. Removes sales pressure.)

OK great. So, in the next 30 days, how much cash flow coming in do you have total? ... Gotcha. And after all expenses, how much do you have left coming in in total? (Cash flow — pacing question, less invasive.)

Sure, cool. And what's your cash on hand exactly right now? ... And that's the exact number you have available? (If they give a round number like 12k, real. If they give a specific number like $500, 99% of the time that's a smoke screen — they're telling you what they can spend in this moment, not what they have.)
And in terms of credit — not saying we have to use it, but just so I have full understanding of how things are looking — what's available to you right now?
And you really wanna do this, right?

OK because look — I don't think the best thing for you to do right now is drop [the full price] and invest all your savings on this or go into credit card debt. But I also know that your business is really important to you, and if you don't do something in the next 6-12 months, I also don't think the best thing to do is nothing. And plus, for you, it's what — [N] clients to break even? So because of that, I'd be willing to let you in for [$X] down — get lead gen going, get clients in. Is that fair? So if that's something I'm willing to do for you — is that something you're willing to move forward with right now?
objections.do_not: Do not offer a payment plan as the rebuttal to uncertainty. Cheaper terms never fix belief. Confirm 'money aside, 100% in' FIRST. Then get permission to explore — don't dive into open wallet without it. Never offer payment plans or discounts before the price drop — they're closing leverage.
alt_reframes: Expensive compared to what, though? 5K for a dinner is expensive; 5K for a car is cheap. Does it really matter what we pay if what we get in return is everything you've ever wanted?

Has 10K always been a lot to you? Do you want it to always be a lot, or do you want to be the kind of person who can move on something that's going to 100% help you? You're never going to get out of the place where 10K is a lot if you make decisions out of your circumstances instead of your vision.

objections.label: I want to think about it / send me the info / I'll get back to you
triggers: get back to you next week
response_steps: No problem. Before we get into any of that — let me ask you this, just because we've been through a lot today. How do you actually feel? Money and everything aside, do you feel like this is 100% what you need to get to [their goal], and that it's 100% going to work?

If they waffle ('I think so'): Got it — but what I'm really trying to understand is, do you think this is 100% going to work, and do you 100% want to do this? It doesn't sound 100% certain — so let's just be honest with each other, what's really going on?

COLE INVERSION: Deliberately mishear the hedge as a no -- 'so it sounds like you don't think it's going to work?' 9/10 they snap back: 'no no, I do think it's going to work.' Lower your tone: 'hold on -- why do you feel like it's going to work?' Now they're selling you on the program in their own words -- closest thing to a self-close. Loop 'why though' on each answer until the real concern surfaces.
If a real concern surfaces, that's the true objection — handle it (route to the matching entry).

If it IS a genuine sleep-on-it: No issue at all, I'd sleep on it too if I were you. So just to clarify — if we schedule a time tomorrow and you wake up feeling the exact same way you feel right now, then what you're telling me is we're 100% processing the payment and moving forward, yes?
Why don't you come in now and draw the line in the sand today — and if you wake up tomorrow and at the bottom of your gut you know it was a terrible decision, we'll just refund you.

JEREMY INVERSION CLOSE (after 3-4 layers of 'why though?'): 'Tell me why you getting [their stated outcome] would be the WRONG thing for you.' They literally cannot answer — they'd have to argue against their own goal. Usually they say 'wait, say that again?' Repeat it slow: 'is [outcome] the right thing or the wrong thing?' Either way they concede → 'why?' They sell themselves.
objections.do_not: Don't accept a vague 'I'll get back to you' and book a loose follow-up. Desire fades. Isolate now, or lock a next-day call with a definitive tie-down.
alt_reframes: CLOSE THE LOOP (Jeremy Miner / Cole): Most of the weight people carry is from open loops, not closed ones. 'Either it's a yes today and the loop closes, or it's a no today and the loop closes. Booking another call to think about it just keeps the loop open. Which is it?'

objections.label: I need to do research / due diligence
triggers: I just found out about you
just found out about you guys
response_steps: No problem at all, happy for you to do that. Just so I can stay organized and get clarity on my end — what's keeping you from being less than 100% certain that this is going to get you to [their outcome]?

So basically what I'm understanding is — you 100% think this will work and you want to move forward, you just want to do a little research to confirm everything I told you checks out. As long as it lines up, you're 100% good to go?
No problem — I can help speed up that research. What specifically do you want to see — reviews, case studies, videos? I can prepare something and send it over.

If they can't name anything specific: Can I be honest with you for a second? Earlier you said you're 100% certain — but when I ask what you want to find out more about, you say nothing in particular. One of my core values is transparency, so I can't help feeling you're just not that into this, which is okay. What's really going on?

objections.label: I need to talk to one of your clients
triggers: talk to one of your clients
speak to one of your clients
talk to some of your clients
do you have clients I can speak to
response_steps: Got it — let's cover that in a second. But just for clarity, aside from that, how do you feel? Do you feel like this is 100% what you need to get to [outcome], and you 100% want to do it?
So theoretically — if you spoke to one of our clients and they validated everything I've told you so far, you're basically good to go, we're processing payment?

Here's our policy: we have 100+ people reaching out every month wanting to become clients. It wouldn't be appropriate or realistic to fill our clients' calendars with people who are still just thinking about joining — especially when our clients are wealthy business owners who charge for their time. That's the exact reason we have 500+ case studies. Is there a specific type of case study you were looking for?

Alternative: If I connect you with a client right after this call, are you 100% okay keeping the exchange to text out of respect for their time? ... And once they echo everything I told you and we talk in 48 hours, what do you think the next step is from there?

objections.label: I need to talk to my spouse / partner / business partner
triggers: need to talk to somebody else
response_steps: No problem. Just so I can be clear — talking to your spouse aside, how do you feel for you personally? Do you feel this is 100% what you need to get to [goal], and that it's 100% going to work?

Cool. So just to clarify — if your spouse was on this call right now and said 'I believe you, do whatever's best for the business,' if they'd already given you that green light, would you be 100% moving forward and processing the payment with me right now?
Aside from letting your spouse know, is there anything else keeping you from being less than 100% certain this is what you need?

Just for clarity's sake — is this a respect thing where you've basically decided and you're just letting them know, or do you genuinely need to sit down, collaborate, and get their permission to move forward?
What do you think they're going to think about this? What will they say when they hear the investment? Are they supportive of you fixing [the problem]? Do they know you're on this call?

There are two ways you can bring this up. One — 'Honey, that business I spent a ton on, I met a guy on the internet, it's 10k, what do you think?' Or two — you sit them down and confidently say 'I've decided and committed to growing this where it should be, and I found someone to help. I'm not asking permission, I'm asking for your emotional support and buy-in.' Which of those two guys do you think convinces his wife? You're right — and if you're not certain, neither will they be, nor should they be.

FUTURE-PACE (Jeremy Miner alternative angle): How does your spouse feel about you losing $[N] a month right now? Is she more stressed about you losing $[N]/month — or about you investing $[X] to fix it? ... How many months are we going to keep pushing this off while you keep losing $[N] a month? (Reframes the spouse from blocker to ally via consequence math.)

Let's put down a refundable deposit now, I'll onboard you, and schedule a call with you, your spouse and me so they can see exactly what you'd be investing in. If they hate it, we refund it. So if I was willing to do that for you, would you be willing to move forward right now?

EXTERNAL-VALIDATION REFRAME (Cole): 'Can I share something? The brain isn't built to thrive, it's built to keep us safe. So when we hit something new, the default is to outsource the decision -- talk to the spouse, the advisor -- so if it doesn't work out, it wasn't our fault. That's not actually about your spouse. That's your brain looking for a way to push this down the road. Real question -- if you take the spouse out of it: do YOU think this works, and do YOU 100% want to do it?'
objections.do_not: Never chase the spouse objection before the prospect themselves is 100% sold. If they're not sold, they cannot sell someone who wasn't on the call.

objections.label: We need to discuss amongst ourselves (3+ partners / decision-makers)
response_steps: Go person by person on the temp check: 'Jim, where are you out of 10? ... Mark, where are you out of 10? ... Alex, looks like you're the only one not certain — it's a two-to-three vote, looks like we're good to go.' You're just closing three people instead of one.

If you can't close on the call: Your partners weren't on this call, so they won't have all the information, and it's a lot for you to relay. Let's schedule a 30-minute call with all of us where I recap everything and re-show them exactly what it looks like to work with us, and all of us decide together.
Lock the tie-down: So when we talk tomorrow, after you've spoken — if you feel the same way you told me you feel right now, then we're 100% moving forward, yes or no?

objections.label: I need to run it by my team / board / CFO (downward authority)
response_steps: If you believe this is the number one constraint in your business, your job as the CEO is to determine the problem, the priority, the vision — and align everyone to attack it. You shouldn't be going to your team asking for permission.
If they say no, are you prepared to tell them, 'Guys, we are doing this'? You're not asking them for permission — you're asking them for buy-in.
If it's genuinely a bandwidth question: get the implementer on a call, or pre-handle it — 'does your team have the bandwidth to implement this this quarter?'

objections.label: I've been burned before / I tried something like this and it didn't work
triggers: how is this going to be different
don't see how this is different
response_steps: Totally get it, that's super frustrating — a lot of times we're picking up the pieces after someone overpromised and underdelivered.
Tell me what happened in that company — what was the difference between what you thought would happen and what was actually implemented?

What we've found, doing this with thousands of clients, is it comes down to one of three things: number one, the process they implemented just didn't work; number two, the strategy was good but the service wasn't — slow, no support; or number three, both were fine and you just didn't show up the way you should have. Which one of those do you think it was?

[They name it — usually method or service] So given the service quality is the same, if the method is right, wouldn't it make sense you wouldn't get the same result as before? So with that out of the way — do you really think this is going to work?

You learned the lesson 'don't work with a beginner' — don't learn the wrong lesson and make it 'this type of thing never works.' That one bad decision is just the tuition you paid to make a better, more informed decision this time. Let's not let one bad decision sabotage a great one.

RE-MEANING (Jeremy Miner -- runs BEFORE the identity-shift): 'You know what's interesting about that? That bad experience didn't break you -- it led you here. Most people would have quit and gone back to a job. You didn't.' Changing the MEANING of the failure from 'evidence this never works' to 'evidence you're built for this.' Re-meaning FIRST, identity-shift SECOND -- doing identity without re-meaning sounds like a glib compliment.

IDENTITY-SHIFT (Jeremy Miner alternative reframe): Sounds like you're the type of entrepreneur who never gives up — you tried [X], it didn't work, and you're still here trying to find a real solution. So why is this so important to you? ... Were you born that way, or did you have to learn it? (Locks the new identity — they can't object without contradicting their new self-image.)

If comparing to a small past provider: You're comparing a 3-person shop with 5 clients and no sales team to a category leader with 3,000+ clients and an 8-figure sales team. How does that comparison even make sense?

EGO-STATE TIE (Jeremy — gender-aware, after the identity affirmation): To a male prospect: 'and your spouse — she's lucky to have a provider like you, someone forward-thinking who makes the hard decisions for the family.' To a female prospect: 'and your spouse — he's lucky to have an independent woman like you who [their move].' Plays to ego state (provider for males, independence for females). Locks the new identity through a witness they care about. ADAPT to what the prospect actually values — some male prospects value being seen as an equal partner over provider; read the signal, don't default-stereotype.
objections.do_not: Don't argue them out of the feeling with a glib analogy ('would you never date again?'). Diagnose what actually happened, then separate it from your offer.

objections.label: Your competitor is cheaper / I'm shopping around / talking to other people
triggers: we're talking to three other guys
response_steps: Quick question before anything else — are you looking for the cheapest option, or are you looking for the team that's most likely to get you there?
Curious — how are you thinking about this? What held you back from going with the other ones?

Ultimately, how would you know if you'd found the right team to help you? ... So it's really just about who's going to get you where you want to go, right? Aside from evaluating which option to go with, it sounds like you're going to do something — it's just a matter of who. So let's take price aside for a moment: out of the two options, which are you more certain can actually get you there?

Can I just be your bro for a sec? You're doing [X], you want to get to [Y]. Whether the investment is five grand or fifty relative to that goal — who gives a damn? Go with the team that's done what you want to do the most amount of times and that you're most sure can get you there.

If the other option is genuinely solid, sequence it instead of trashing it: come work with us first to get the foundation right, and if you still want to, go work with that guy in three months. And just so you know what to watch for — a team that won't even let you go talk to other programs first, that's a red flag.

WHAT THEY'LL SAY (Jeremy Miner): What are you hoping that other company is going to say? ... Do you think they're going to say they're worse than us? Of course not — every salesperson says they're the best. So what's that really telling you?

INTUITION CLOSE (Jeremy Miner): Let's say their proposal looks similar to ours and the price is similar. How would you actually decide who to go with? ... Your intuition? OK — what does your intuition say right now? ... Why?

DELIVERY (Cole/Jeremy): As you contrast their option vs yours, physically separate your hands -- their option here, your option there. Even on audio the gesture changes your tone enough for the prospect to feel the split. Sitting still flattens the frame. 'Selling from stage they point to the doors -- same thing on a phone.'

BINARY FORCE (Cole, role-play 2): 'Is the cheapest price the most important thing to you, or actually like scaling your company to $[goal]?' Force the binary — they can't logically pick 'cheapest.' Then anchor the ROI ratio: 'Because whether it's 10K or 20K, the result is 10x that either way if it works.' Collapses 'shopping' from price-comparison frame into outcome-comparison.
objections.do_not: Don't trash the competitor — bulldozing makes you look like 'just a closer.' Educate on the options instead. If a competitor is genuinely solid, sequence it: 'come work with us first, then go work with that guy in 3 months.'

objections.label: I want to start later / after the holidays / next quarter / after my trip
triggers: want to do it in two months
response_steps: Got it. So timing aside — you're 100% in?
Just to be clear — if we're having this exact conversation on [their start date] and you feel the same way, you're 100% giving me your credit card and moving forward?

Well, I've got an idea — are you open to it? I don't think the best thing for you is to wait and do nothing. But I also don't think the best thing is to hop in when you can't fully commit. So what I'd be willing to do is add 30 days onto your engagement — you start now, knock out the onboarding, and when your official start date comes we hit the ground running. So if I was willing to do that for you, would you be willing to move forward right now?

If it's a trip: honestly the timing's perfect — on a long flight you'll have time to knock out the onboarding and training you wouldn't have working full-time. I'll set your official start date for [date] and buy you extra time in the program.

objections.label: I don't have time to implement this right now
response_steps: No problem. So timing aside — is there anything else keeping you from being less than 100% certain?

Can I tell you what I'm seeing? You told me the number one problem in your business is [their constraint]. And your bottleneck to solving it is time. But the reason you don't have time IS [the constraint]. So the very problem you got on this call to solve is the exact thing keeping you from getting started — you're in a self-perpetuating loop, you're stuck.
So the real problem isn't time, it's a mix-up of priorities. You've already identified [the constraint] as the problem and this as the best way to fix it — so isn't this your number one priority?

I'm not asking you to work more hours — I'm asking you to direct the hours you already have into the number one constraint in your business. If you're going to grow it, why would you not focus on this now? If not now, when?

You make time to go to the gym and be healthy — it's not a question. What you really need is one to two hours a day. Is it genuinely impossible for you to wake up an hour earlier or go to bed an hour later?

objections.label: Nerves / fear — they're 100% in but freeze, or it's 'a big decision'
triggers: hard for me to make a decision
this is a lot to take in
response_steps: Release the pressure: Can I ask you a personal question? There's probably something else going through your head. We've been talking a while, and from my end everything about this makes sense for you. Will you just open up and tell me what you're thinking — what's really going on?

Name it: It just seems like it's a little bit of nerves. Is it? ... Good — the nerves are good. That means there's weight to this, there's meaning to it. I'd think you were an alien if you weren't a little nervous. Nothing great in the world was ever built by someone who wasn't a little nervous at first.

Identity: So the nerves are really irrelevant here. The real question is — who do you want to be? The type of person who feels the fear and does it anyway, or the type who lets nervousness make the decision? Which is it?

Can I ask you a weird question — does it feel like your head and your heart are playing tug-of-war? Your brain is trying to keep you safe, it's yelling at you not to do it — but your heart is the thing that lit up when you told me what [outcome] would mean. Which one do you think will take you farther?

There are two parts to your brain — the monkey brain that keeps you safe, and the part that wants you to succeed. How many people do you know who knew about Bitcoin in 2010 and did nothing? They listened to the monkey brain. Listen to the part that's going to make you successful.

objections.label: What if it doesn't work for me / I don't think it'll work
triggers: I'll be the one it doesn't work for
how do I know this works
response_steps: Just so I can stay organized — what you're saying is, despite the hundreds of case studies and the [X]% success rate, you're worried you'll be the small percentage this doesn't work for, right?

Can I ask you an honest question? If you come in and do this — number one, are you 100% going to put in the work? And number two, when you hit a snag, are you going to raise your hand and ask for help, or bury your head in the sand?

So if we have a 90%+ success rate for people who do the work, and you're 100% going to put in the work, and you promise you'll raise your hand when you need help — then tell me, why wouldn't this work for you?

If I hand you the best camping gear with a big guarantee on it — who still has to fill the canteen with water and walk the trail? You. So the real question isn't about the program — it's whether you're committed to being the person who gets the result from it.

objections.label: Is there a guarantee?
response_steps: We can definitely talk about that. Just curious — is there a specific reason you're asking? (This sniffs out the hidden objection behind it — usually 'I've been burned.')

Honestly, there's a lot that's out of our control — like, are you going to put in the work? Me guaranteeing a specific result would be illegal, immoral and unethical anyway. What I CAN guarantee is that we'll give you every tool and resource you need to get [the outcome], and that we have an impeccable track record.

What really matters is two things: are you going to 100% show up and do the work, and when you hit a problem — which you will — are you going to raise your hand for help? ... Great question, what else?

objections.label: It's too risky / too big a risk / too good to be true
response_steps: I hear you on that. Can I give you a little coaching on it? ... Your goal is to make [X] a year — that would put you in the top 1%. Have you ever wondered why so few people make that kind of money despite wanting it? It's the fear of risk.

So the real question isn't 'is this too risky' — the real question is who do you want to be? When 99% of people bump into that glass wall of fear and risk, they contract and retreat to their comfort zone — which is exactly what keeps them where they are. The 1% feel the fear and break through.
So which of those two people do you want to be?

objections.label: I'll just do it myself / try it on my own first
triggers: try it on my own first
I'll just try it and see
response_steps: Use their own words against the objection: 'Wait — earlier on the call you told me [what they said about being stuck / having tried]. Now you're saying you'll do it on your own. What's really going on?'

You've been trying to figure this out for [time] — I'm not saying you can't do it, you likely have every capability you need. So the question isn't can you or can't you. The question is: what's the fastest, most probable path that stacks everything in your favor?

Curse-of-knowledge reframe (for agency/expert prospects): The classic saying is 'I'm great at getting results for my clients but not for myself.' That's not your fault — it's just the curse of knowledge. If I were you, I'd hedge the bet the most in my favor.
Why would you want to use a proven pathway? Because it requires less mental and financial resources to get there faster than figuring it out alone.

objections.label: It sounds good but I need to see it first
triggers: don't know until I see it
response_steps: That's totally fine. Help me understand — when you say 'see it,' what exactly are you looking to see, just so I can help?
Yeah, no worries — let me share my screen right now. I'll walk you through the training portal and give you a glimpse inside the community so you can see exactly what it looks like to be a client.
(Note: 'I need to see it' usually means they just can't picture what working with you looks like — so show them.)

objections.label: I never make same-day decisions / I always sleep on big decisions
triggers: don't make decisions on the first call
response_steps: Can I tell you what I think we should do? Let's put down a refundable deposit — I'll fully onboard you, and if at any moment what I told you we'd deliver isn't in alignment with what you're getting, I'll give you a 100% refund, because we didn't uphold our end. So it's a no-risk decision.
Help me understand — if it's a no-risk decision and you're a 10 out of 10, what would hold you back from just moving forward?
The way you've made decisions in the past created the results you have now — the exact results you're on this call to change. To change them, we have to change the pattern of how you make decisions.
You said you want to make an informed decision — but the only informed decision you can make is from the inside, actually seeing the product. Are you more informed from the inside or the outside?

objections.label: Why should I trust you / how do I know you're legit
triggers: why is it you I should trust
how do I know this is real
response_steps: B2C: [Name], totally hear you. Here's what I'm going to do — I'm sending you a text right now. Did you get it? Great, that's my personal cell. When I say I care about your success, I mean it — any time you're a client, if you need anything, text or call me. I've got your back, I'm not going to let you fail.
B2B: [Big-name clients] trusted us. Do you think they don't know how to make good buying decisions? Of course they do. You should trust this too.
Reframe the rep's own mindset: if prospects keep feeling 'untrustworthy of you,' you may be pushing too hard and making them defensive. Lead supportive, not combative.

objections.label: Do you have a payment plan? / Can we break it into payments?
triggers: can we do a two pay
response_steps: Don't just give it. First confirm: 'When you're on a call and a client has the money, needs it, and knows they need it — do you think they should break it into two? ... So money aside, you're 100% in?'
Run the open wallet (30-day cash → cash on hand exactly → credit) to find the biggest plan they can comfortably and ethically do.

Then trade the concession for a decision: 'I don't think the best thing for you is to drain your savings, but I also don't think the best thing is to do nothing. So what I'd be willing to do is let you in for [half] down — and if I'm willing to do that for you, are you willing to move forward right now?'
If you have to go lower again, ask for more back: 'If I'm willing to do that for you, will you move forward right now AND give me a case study when you get amazing results?'
objections.do_not: Never blurt 'what about a two-pay?' or hand over a plan free. A concession with no exchange has no value. Always trade it for a decision.

objections.label: I'm 100% in, I just need to move money around / wait for a payment
triggers: pay in full in a couple days
response_steps: Okay, walk me through it real fast so I can stay organized. When you say you're moving money around — what does that look like? Where's it coming from? Selling stocks, a 401k, a brokerage account?
And when is that going to be finished? ... And once it's done, you're 100% moving forward that day?

Then let's do the bulk of it now — say seven-and-a-half of the ten — that way we still get you onboarded, get the assessment, get the forms and the onboarding call out of the way, and we just take care of the rest in a week when you're done moving the money around. (You're already 100% in and the money is real — take most of it now, not half.)

Gentleman's agreement: Let's get this done now so you get access to everything and knock out the onboarding forms — just make me a gentleman's agreement that you'll have the rest down before your onboarding call.

objections.label: Let me make some money first, then I'll buy
triggers: do this other thing first then come back
response_steps: Can I be really honest? If you had the winning lottery ticket, don't you think you'd have cashed it in by now? If you had the ability to change your situation and make more money, you'd have done it already — and we wouldn't be on this phone. Do you agree?
If you had all the tools you needed to change [their circumstance], you would have already changed it. So waiting to 'make money first' is waiting for the exact thing this is designed to fix.

objections.label: I'm not allowed to / not interested in buying a coaching program
response_steps: Based on what we covered, we can definitely help. I know you said you're not interested in a coaching program — but you just told me [what they said they want / their pain], and I know we can help you get [core desired result], because we've done it for [case study, case study, case study].

So if you're open, I can walk you through what the program is and how it helps you — but I want this to be a serious conversation where you're actually considering it, otherwise we're both wasting our time. So where do you want to go from here?

objections.label: Just get to the price / just tell me what you've got (prospect taking control)
triggers: just tell me what you got
I get sold all the time
just tell me how it works
response_steps: I'm totally prepared to share what we have going on and how we might help if it makes sense. But everything we do is customized — so at this stage what makes the most sense is let me get a little context on your business: your market, how you're generating leads now, what's going on with your team. Then I can share the parts of what we do that are relevant and useful to you specifically. That's the most time-efficient way — is that cool?

Take responsibility for the conversation if it slipped: 'Oh, I totally apologize, I think I misheard something — that's my bad. So the main thing is [their problem] — how are you currently [doing the thing] right now?'
Match their energy: if they're super direct, be super direct back. Stay calm, stay in the lead, treat it as a fun puzzle, not a threat.

objections.label: Prospect is waffling / won't name a concern / 'I think so'
triggers: it's just a lot to think about
I just need to process this
response_steps: Cut in playfully and call out the tonality: 'I think so? That doesn't sound 100% certain — so let's just be honest with each other for a second, what's really going on?'

Man, can I ask you a personal question? There's probably something else going through your head. From my end everything about this makes sense for you. Will you just open up and tell me what you're thinking?

Just level with me — what's really going on? Earlier you said you wanted to do this, you said it sounds really good. If you do it now or later that's fine, but it feels like something's on your mind we haven't discussed. If we're going to work together, we have to be honest with each other. So what's really going on?
Feed them the objection if they still can't name it: 'It just sounds like it's a little bit of nerves — is it?' Then handle nerves.
objections.do_not: Don't let a vague 'I think so' slide into a booked follow-up. Turn the intangible into a tangible objection you can actually handle.

objections.label: Are you offering any discounts?
triggers: can you do better on price
response_steps: No. (There's nothing more you need to say than that. Don't do fast-action discounts or incentive-based pricing — they're a closing crutch and they cheapen the offer.)

Quote the price as a flat statement and then go silent — 'the investment to get your business to [outcome] is just [price].' Do not fill the pause with a softener or a payment plan. Let the silence sit.

If pressed, redirect to value, never to price: re-anchor the price to the outcome, and ask the binary — 'are you looking for the cheapest option, or a premium-quality option?' Keep the investment simple and fixed; payment terms (not discounts) are the only lever, and only after isolating a true financial objection.

objections.label: Send me the recording / a summary / email me and I'll review it
triggers: review it on my own time
response_steps: No problem. Before I do that — let me ask you this: money and everything aside, do you feel like this is 100% what you need to get to [their goal], and that it's 100% going to work?

Here's what I've found — a recording without me there to answer the questions that come up usually just sits there. So let's not let that happen to you. What's the real thing you'd be reviewing for — is there something specific you're still not sure about?

If a real concern surfaces, that's the true objection — handle it. If there isn't one, don't book a loose follow-up: 'It sounds like you're 100% there. Let's just get you started — what's your billing address?'
If they genuinely need a hard next step: lock a specific time tomorrow with a definitive tie-down — 'when we talk at [time], if you feel the same way, we're 100% moving forward, yes?'
objections.do_not: Don't treat this like 'think about it' and isolate certainty for ten minutes — and don't just send a recording into the void. This is the post-call-disappearance setup. Either close now or lock a hard, tied-down next step.

objections.label: I'll get back to you — flat exit / hand on the doorknob
triggers: let me get back to you
I'll think it through and let you know
response_steps: Read the tonality. If they've clearly already decided and are just being polite, don't run another temp-check loop — use the honest takeaway.
TAKEAWAY: 'Can I be totally straight with you? It feels like this is a no — and that's completely okay, I'd rather you tell me than disappear. Be honest with me: it's a no, isn't it?'

This usually does one of two things — it either gets a real 'yes it's a no' (so you can ask the one question that surfaces the real reason: 'fair enough — what was the thing that didn't land?'), or it snaps them back: 'no, no, it's not that...' — and now the real objection is on the table.
Whatever they name, handle it through diffuse -> isolate. Do not accept a vague exit.
objections.do_not: Don't book a polite follow-up call you both know won't happen. A flat 'I'll get back to you' is a no being delivered gently — call it, with respect, so you get a real answer.

objections.label: Post-close cold feet / can I cancel / I'm not sure I should have done this
response_steps: Diffuse and stay calm — do not panic or get defensive: 'Totally hear you, and I'm glad you told me instead of sitting on it. Talk to me — what came up?'

Re-anchor to why they bought: 'Earlier you told me [their goal / their pain] and that this was exactly what you needed. None of that changed in the last ten minutes — so what's actually going on right now?'
Name it as nerves if that's what it is: 'This is the monkey brain doing its job — the moment after a big decision is when fear shouts loudest. That doesn't mean it was the wrong decision.'
Re-confirm the decision and move them into action fast: 'Let's get you into onboarding right now and book your first call — momentum is what kills the doubt. You good?'
objections.do_not: Don't ignore post-close remorse hoping it passes, and don't immediately offer the refund. The deal isn't safe until cash clears and onboarding starts — reassure, re-anchor, and move them into action.
